practice.title: Admire Wisdom Fear
agreedSteps: Meditate on the benefits of developing wisdom fear. Admire what it does for the mind until you naturally wish to develop it; once you see what you'll get from it, these meditations become simple.

Whenever a negative experience arises, use it to learn about karma: this is the consequence of not practicing Dharma at some point in the past, and it shows there is more of that karma in my mind. Let it motivate you both to purify and to practice virtue.
When you look at suffering and its causes, remember it isn't heavy, it's important. Like a parent teaching a child about traffic, just be clear: this matters, and I'm not going to turn away from it.
steps: Ask yourself: what specific problems in my life does wisdom fear solve that I can't solve without it?

Check your practice for purity. Is there an underlying motivation of pleasure, reputation, praise, or just making this life comfortable? Make your immediate aim to practice purely, not to get results; the results will come naturally.

Read Geshe-la's lines as a daily affirmation: It makes no difference whether or not I receive respect, a good reputation, or praise. I do not receive any great benefit from these, and when I lose them, I am not greatly harmed. Words of blame cannot hurt me. Wealth is easily lost, and the pleasures of this life are transient. I do not need to be so interested in these things, or overly concerned about them.
When thinking about suffering makes you unhappy or bored, ask: what is my attachment trying to protect me from here?
Fold wisdom fear into the project you're already working on rather than starting a separate one.
practice.quote: No, this is important. I'm not going to turn away from this until I have a realization.

commentary.title: Wisdom Fear
content: Ordinary fear is totally meaningless. It just makes us miserable, anxious and worried. Wisdom fear is different: it gives great meaning to our life. From one point of view it's a kind of non-attachment, and from another it morphs naturally into refuge, because refuge is basically a combination of fear and faith. If there were no dangers of samsara and lower rebirth, there'd be no point in going for refuge.

When a danger is evident, our mind automatically looks for protection. If you're in the back of a bodega and someone comes in with a gun, you don't just think, oh no, a gun, and stay stuck there. You instantly think, where can I go for protection? That's the psychological response we want wisdom fear to produce.

As we go through these six points of conscientiousness, we want to arrive at the feeling: I really want wisdom fear. I see its value, and I see the specific problems in my life it would solve that I cannot solve otherwise. That makes it very appealing; we think, I need this.
commentary.quote: So ordinary fear is meaningless. [...] Wisdom fear gives great meaning to our life.

commentary.title: Infinite Negative Karma
content: Buddha taught that a moment of evil leads to rebirth in the lowest hell for many eons. That doesn't mean it's literally impossible to get out of the lower realms. We have a human life now, and we've been in the lower realms before. But probabilistically the chance is so close to zero that it's good to think, basically, I'm not getting out, at least not for an unbelievably long time.

There is basically infinite negative karma in the mind. It isn't all ripening right now, but once we take a lower rebirth those seeds keep germinating, and it's very hard to stop the cycle. Think about being born as a spider: your whole life is trapping living beings, paralyzing them in mortal fear, injecting venom, wrapping them up alive. It's the only way the spider can stay alive, and it doesn't have the complexity of mind to think, I'll stop killing and purify this. How do you get out of that?

But we don't want to stop at the analysis, or there's no outlet for it and it's just scary. The analysis is a bridge to virtuous minds: non-attachment, refuge, a wish to purify, and especially regret. Our job is to prevent lower rebirth through purification and by liberating our mind swiftly.
commentary.quote: What we're trying to do is use the analysis as a bridge to virtuous minds.

commentary.title: No One Is Coming
content: Merely experiencing the sufferings of the lower realms doesn't lead to release, because while we're there we create even more non-virtue. No one is sentenced to a time after which they're automatically released from samsara. Those who've achieved liberation did it by uprooting the cause, not by waiting for their misery to run out.

This opposes a delusion that says, I can just wait it out. We do this in life all the time: I'll wait for them to forgive me, for the situation to get better on its own, for the world to get better. That's a passive approach, a little like thinking someone in control will make it all work out one day. If Buddha could do that for us, he would have already done it.

Buddha said you are your own friend, you are your own enemy, you are your own protector. This is radical responsibility. We're patient when we're doing the right thing, but we're not just waiting for things to wrap up. Our mind is actively creating what's going on, so it can actively create something new. That's empowering.

There's no real happiness in samsara, from the poorest beggar to the most exalted world leader. The first note of this life is a newborn's shriek of pain. Imagine going to the orchestra and that's the opening note; you'd think, that's some foreshadowing.
commentary.quote: There's no one coming to save us, to make it better, to get us out of our situation.

commentary.title: Clear Consequences, Clear Mind
content: To truly value Dharma, it's not enough to think about the good things it brings. We have to think about the bad things it prevents. Something only becomes really appealing when its benefits are juxtaposed with the bad things it prevents. We live in a world of toxic positivity. Buddhists are utterly optimistic about nirvana and utterly pessimistic about samsara. If we only stay in the positive, everything blows out and looks the same, and our practice becomes airy and disembodied.

When we only think about the positive, it feels like the choice is between virtue and something neutral, so virtue becomes a little cherry on top that's competing for our time. When we see the consequences clearly, we understand the choice is really between virtue and suffering. Then there's no inner conflict, no feeling of being a fraud or a hypocrite who can't live their ideal. Practice stops feeling optional, and that's actually very comforting.

Think about New York City driving: millions of death machines whipping around, people on their phones, bikes and pedestrians everywhere, and almost no one directing traffic. What creates the order? The consequences of hitting someone are so obvious that they put everyone inside a certain boundary. Imagine if the laws of karma were that clear in our mind. We'd just know what to do and what not to do, and we'd get on with it. That's the inner alignment wisdom fear brings.
commentary.quote: When the negative consequences of something become very clear, the mind becomes very clear.

commentary.title: Important, Not Heavy
content: Wisdom fear drives us toward conscientiousness and mindfulness, toward a mind that cherishes virtue and abandons non-virtue. We're thinking about awful things that are realities, but the result is a deeply peaceful mind.

Many of us squirm when these subjects come up, or feel blank and bored. Thinking about suffering in the name of developing wisdom fear doesn't make us unhappy; the unhappiness and the boredom come from attachment. Our psychic defense mechanisms don't want to abandon our own prison, so they wrap us in a cocoon. When that happens, ask: what is my attachment trying to protect me from? It's threatened by my path to liberation, but actually attachment is my real threat.

We don't need to make this heavy. Heaviness comes from being attached to some status quo we feel is being threatened. A parent teaching a child about traffic isn't walking around in mourning all day; they're just clear: if you run in the street you'll get hurt, this is important, stop. That connotation of heaviness is just self-cherishing looking for an excuse to get out of doing the work. Engage with it rawly and directly, without denial and without the walls up.
commentary.quote: Heaviness is always just the attachment.

commentary.title: Practice Purely, Not for Results
content: In Joyful Path, Geshe-la explains that while we're attached to resources, respect, pleasure, reputation and praise, our mind is unbalanced: overexcited when we have them, dejected when we lose them. We want a mind with little ups and downs like a pebble in a pond, not crashing waves, and a peace that's independent of things going well or badly. Death meditation is what really brings this balance.

Read Geshe-la's lines like an affirmation every day: it makes no difference whether or not I receive respect, a good reputation, or praise; words of blame cannot hurt me; wealth is easily lost. We won't mean it at first, but saying it starts attuning us to the balanced mind the death meditation leads to.

If we've practiced for some time without feeling the benefits, it's because we're not yet practicing purely. In the beginning our aspiration shouldn't be to gain results; it should be to practice purely, and the results will come in their own time. When someone says, I meditated but didn't feel anything, they often mean they didn't get a pleasurable hit. That isn't the point. Meditation creates the karma for peace. And using meditation only to make this life cozy, as the best coping mechanism ever, is aiming at samsara rather than liberation.

When death awareness combines with Powa practice, the practitioner actually becomes happy to die, joyful, because they see the reality of their future life in the Pure Land and know the pathway there. Thinking about death brings relaxation about this life, and Powa provides the insurance for what comes after.
commentary.quote: That's basically using it as a samsara improvement project. It's not a liberation project.

commentary.title: What Wisdom Fear Solves
content: Wisdom fear increases mindfulness and concentration, and it fuels renunciation; attachment won't really get the boot until we have renunciation, and we don't get renunciation without wisdom fear.

It gives us a long-term view. The problems of future lives are so much greater than the problems of this life that this life's problems start to pale and stop bothering us. That creates a new problem, but one that's solved by training our mind, not by trying to control external things, which is what makes us so anxious. Being driven inward like this is very healing.

It also protects our concentration and makes us hungry for the three higher trainings. Concentration is our seed of Buddhahood, and it's what will help us understand emptiness directly. The bodhisattva paths are paths of concentration; the path of accumulation begins with tranquil abiding on bodhichitta.
commentary.quote: The problems of future lives can only be solved with Dharma.

commentary.title: When Nothing Can Be Done
content: Situations on the outside that are painful and that we can do absolutely nothing about are actually very helpful. When we can control or scheme about something, we get obsessed with problem solving and the external solution. When there's nothing we can do, all we can do is practice Dharma. We have to put down the need for control.

This is what Kadampa Buddhism is about: mixing Dharma with daily life. When Milarepa was asked which pure land he attained enlightenment in, he pointed to his cave. People saw a ratty old dude in a dirty cave, but his mind was perceiving a pure land. We don't get there by separating our practice from our daily life. The fifth chapter is the mindfulness chapter, and the rest of this chapter is ramping us up for it.
commentary.quote: So all I can do is practice Dharma right now. It's the only recourse.

commentary.title: Exchanging Self with Others
content: To exchange self with others, we need to completely forget the old us. A helpful way is to view the old us as a distinct other, seeing that person from a new mind's eye, even replaying an interaction from the other person's point of view. When that feeling really lands, most of the self-grasping drops out, which is why exchanging and meditation on emptiness are so close.

Then make sure the exercise funnels into a virtuous mind: a cherishing love or a strong compassion that wants to protect them. When we feel that one person's suffering is too much and we can't help, imagine that times billions of beings, including those in the hells, the hungry spirits and the animals. The mind gets funneled into the wish to become enlightened.
commentary.quote: So we don't want to necessarily just stop at thinking, what's it like to be you from your point of view?

dataShares: Alexis remembered the advice to listen to Dharma for at least 30 consecutive minutes, tried it when caught in a self-focused mood, and felt really great. KK: it's the sustained focus that has cumulative benefits.

Adriana listed six people she considers enemies and traced her dislike down to a humility and jealousy problem in her own mind, not a problem with the people. KK affirmed the exercise: it's the state of mind toward the people that's the job.
Suzanne applied the traveler mindset to worries about her apartment, which led her to precious human life and a wish to be more mindful and present in daily tasks.

Sumit worked with his miserliness project after a vivid dream, sitting with the painful possibility of losing someone he's attached to; it pushed him into a mind of love. KK noted that situations we can't control leave Dharma as the only recourse.

Mimi tried the three columns from last week and saw how she grasped at colleagues' messages as inherently hurtful. KK: taking one instance and seeing the gap between what we assert and how we live motivates us to close it.

Neil is working to bring patience and compassion consciously into his work day rather than keeping Dharma in the morning. KK pointed to Milarepa and the Kadampa way of mixing practice with daily life.

Kristin found death meditation helps with never-ending to-do lists and prioritizing, and practiced exchanging self with others in a hard situation at work but didn't reach joy. KK suggested viewing the old self as other and funneling the feeling into love or compassion.

On what wisdom fear solves: Anne is folding it into her cessation-of-distractions project as fuel for mindfulness and concentration; Fran found it helps her see the attachment mixed in with compassion when a loved one is struggling; Mimi sees it pushing her toward renunciation; Jose said it gives a long-term view; Dale said it makes other things seem trivial and protects the peace of concentration.
For the week: Anne will meditate on the benefits of wisdom fear; Jose suggested treating negative experiences as lessons in karma; Fran added that this isn't heavy, just important.
